review_status: Coverage-complete catalogue for all 150 syllabus outcomes. Existing ids are stable; add items rather than renaming ids already in use. Teacher review remains recommended as new student evidence is collected.
basis: Cambridge O Level Mathematics (Syllabus D) 4024 syllabus for 2025-2027, version 2
Observable errors represented by the curated question bank and official mark schemes
Recurring candidate errors described in Cambridge 4024 principal examiner reports for 2022-2024

items.description: Moves a term to the other side of an equation without changing its sign
Uses the wrong inverse operation, for example subtracting a coefficient instead of dividing by it
Applies an operation to only one side, or only one term, of an equation
Multiplies only the first term inside a bracket
Does not change every sign when expanding a bracket preceded by a minus sign
Squares or multiplies binomials without the middle terms, for example (a + b)² = a² + b²
Combines unlike terms, such as x and x², or ab and a
Leaves a common factor inside the brackets, so the expression is not fully factorised
Chooses factor pairs with the wrong signs when factorising a quadratic
Misapplies the difference of two squares, for example factorising a² + b² or writing (a - b)²
Cancels individual terms instead of common factors in an algebraic fraction
Adds numerators and denominators separately or uses an incorrect common denominator
Multiplies only part of a numerator when writing fractions over a common denominator
Multiplies indices when multiplying powers, or adds indices when raising a power to a power
Treats a negative index as a negative number instead of a reciprocal
Confuses the root and the power in a fractional index
Applies a power to the variable but not the coefficient, for example (3x)² = 3x²
Factorises or uses the formula before rearranging the quadratic to equal zero
Makes a sign or bracket error when substituting into the quadratic formula
Gives x = a instead of x = -a from a factor (x + a) = 0
Adds equations when they should be subtracted, or the reverse, when eliminating a variable
Finds only one unknown or one root and stops
Does not reverse the inequality sign after multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Uses the wrong open or closed circle, or broken or solid line, for a strict or inclusive inequality
Shades the opposite side of a boundary from the required region, or describes the region with reversed inequalities
Uses the common difference as the nth term or omits the adjusting constant, for example 3n instead of 3n + 2
Confuses a term's value with its position in the sequence
Uses the given values directly without finding the constant of proportionality, or uses the wrong power
Treats inverse proportion as direct proportion
Calculates gradient as horizontal change over vertical change
Misreads the scale or a value on a graph axis
Uses the wrong area formula, or a gradient, for distance under a speed-time graph
Substitutes correctly but evaluates in the wrong order, for example -3² instead of (-3)²
Gives the reciprocal 1/f(x) instead of the inverse function, or reverses operations in the wrong order
Applies the functions in the wrong order for a composite function
Mixes units, such as dollars and cents, when forming an equation
Writes the stated relationship backwards when forming an expression or equation
Removes a square, square root or power in the wrong order when changing the subject
Classifies 1 as a prime number instead of recognising that a prime has exactly two positive factors
Confuses factors with multiples when listing or using them
Classifies a terminating or recurring decimal as irrational, or a non-terminating non-recurring value as rational
Finds a negative, opposite or additive inverse instead of the multiplicative reciprocal
Uses the union region for an intersection, or the intersection region for a union
Uses element and subset notation interchangeably
Counts or places elements in both sets without accounting for the intersection
Takes a complement without restricting it to the stated universal set
Uses a power when a root is required, or a root when a power is required
Ignores the effect of brackets and exponent parity when raising a negative number to a power
Gives both positive and negative values for a principal square root, or treats a negative square as positive without brackets
Reverses the roles of numerator and denominator when representing a fraction
Converts between mixed and improper fractions without multiplying the whole number by the denominator
Moves the decimal point by the wrong number of places when converting between decimals and percentages
Converts a fraction to a decimal using the digits rather than division or place value
Orders negative numbers by their absolute values and therefore reverses their true order
Uses the greater-than or less-than symbol in the wrong direction for the stated order
Evaluates every operation strictly from left to right instead of applying the order of operations
Divides fractions without multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor
Applies an incorrect sign rule when adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing negative numbers
Aligns the final digits rather than decimal points when adding or subtracting decimals
Treats a non-zero base raised to the power zero as zero instead of one
Applies multiplication index laws to a sum or difference of powers
Leaves the leading coefficient outside the interval from 1 inclusive to 10 exclusive
Uses a positive exponent for a small number or a negative exponent for a large number
Adds or subtracts coefficients while the powers of ten are different
Combines the powers of ten with the wrong operation when multiplying or dividing standard-form values
Rounds to decimal places when significant figures are requested, or the reverse
Uses a digit other than the first discarded digit to decide whether to round up
Calculates with the original values or rounds inconsistently instead of choosing simple compatible approximations
Rounds an intermediate value too early and makes the final answer inaccurate
Reports a calculator value to an unjustified or impractical precision for the context
Uses the full rounding unit instead of half the unit to form lower and upper bounds
Treats both endpoints as included or gives the rounded value itself as a bound
Combines both lower bounds or both upper bounds without considering which combination minimises or maximises the result
Uses rounded measurements as exact values instead of calculating with their bounds
Treats one ratio part as the whole, or forms a part-to-whole ratio when a part-to-part ratio is required
Forms or simplifies a ratio before converting both quantities to the same units
Divides a quantity by one ratio number instead of by the sum of all ratio parts
Uses an additive change where the relationship requires multiplication by a scale factor
Divides the rate quantities in the reverse order, such as time divided by distance for speed
Combines rate quantities expressed in incompatible units without conversion
Finds the arithmetic mean of separate speeds instead of total distance divided by total time
Uses a percentage as a whole number rather than converting it to a decimal or multiplier
Uses the comparison value instead of the required original or whole quantity as the percentage base
Divides the change by the new value instead of the original value
Reports the final account balance when interest is requested, or reports only the interest when the balance is requested
Applies each percentage change to the original amount instead of the updated amount
Subtracts the stated percentage from the final amount instead of dividing by the final percentage multiplier
Enters a multi-part numerator, denominator or exponent without the brackets needed to preserve its structure
Uses radians or another calculator angle mode when the question uses degrees
Truncates, rounds or copies the calculator display incorrectly
Calculates with hours and minutes as decimal base-ten units, such as treating 1.30 hours as 1 hour 30 minutes
Multiplies when converting to a larger time unit or divides when converting to a smaller one
Subtracts clock digits directly and mishandles borrowing across an hour or across midnight
Converts noon, midnight, am or pm incorrectly between 12-hour and 24-hour time
Reads an arrival or departure time as a journey duration, or uses the wrong row or column
Treats major and minor currency units inconsistently or gives an invalid number of minor-unit digits
Multiplies when the quoted exchange rate requires division, or divides when it requires multiplication
Misidentifies which currency one unit of the quoted exchange rate refers to
Adds or subtracts a fixed amount each period instead of applying a repeated multiplicative change
Uses a growth multiplier for decay, a decay multiplier for growth, or changes the percentage in the wrong direction
Adds or subtracts unlike surds as though their radicands were the same
Fails to identify and extract the largest square factor when simplifying a surd
Multiplies or divides surds by operating on coefficients and radicands inconsistently
Multiplies only the denominator or leaves a surd in the denominator after rationalising
Uses the same binomial instead of the conjugate, or expands the conjugate product with the wrong signs
Treats a letter as a fixed label or object rather than a number that can vary or be generalised
Reads adjacent letters or a coefficient and letter as concatenated digits rather than multiplication
Uses a term-to-term rule as though it directly gives the nth term, or the reverse
Assumes a sequence is arithmetic from its first change and ignores a changing difference or other pattern
Plots a point with its horizontal and vertical coordinates interchanged
Joins discrete points or categorical data as a continuous curve, or fails to join continuous data appropriately
Draws or interprets exponential change as having a constant additive difference or straight-line graph
Draws an exponential graph crossing its horizontal asymptote without the function requiring it
Sketches a quadratic without the correct symmetry, turning point orientation or intercept pattern
Draws a reciprocal graph crossing an axis that is an asymptote
Reads or writes a coordinate as vertical then horizontal instead of horizontal then vertical
Assigns the wrong signs to coordinates in a Cartesian quadrant
Draws a straight-line graph from an unreliable single point or from two incorrectly calculated points without checking
Forces a line through the origin or through plotted points that do not satisfy the given equation
Gives a positive gradient for a line that falls from left to right, or a negative gradient for one that rises
Subtracts the coordinates in different point orders in the numerator and denominator of the gradient
Adds the horizontal and vertical changes instead of using Pythagoras to find the straight-line distance
Uses raw coordinate values or unsquared differences in the distance formula
Halves the coordinate differences without adding them to a starting point, instead of averaging corresponding coordinates
Averages one coordinate pair but copies or subtracts the other pair
Interchanges the gradient and vertical intercept when using the form y = mx + c
Writes y = mx without finding a non-zero intercept from a point on the line
Changes the gradient of a parallel line instead of keeping it equal to the given line's gradient
Copies both gradient and intercept, producing the same line rather than the required distinct parallel line
Uses the same gradient or only changes its sign for a perpendicular line
Takes a reciprocal without changing its sign when finding a perpendicular gradient
Describes intersecting perpendicular lines as parallel, or parallel lines as perpendicular
Treats similar shapes as necessarily equal in size, or congruent shapes as allowing a non-unit scale factor
Uses an exterior angle where an interior angle is required, or the reverse
Infers equal, parallel or perpendicular sides from how a shape looks rather than from its markings or properties
Uses a diameter as a radius or a radius as a diameter
Misidentifies a chord, tangent, secant or arc and applies a property to the wrong circle feature
Reads the wrong protractor scale or measures from the wrong zero
Draws a triangle by estimating angles or measuring all points instead of intersecting compass arcs from the given side lengths
Draws construction arcs from incorrect centres or with radii that do not match the given sides
Places faces in a net so that they overlap, leave a gap or cannot meet on folding
Omits or duplicates a face because it is not visible in the solid's drawing
Multiplies when converting drawing length to actual length where division is required, or the reverse
Measures a bearing anticlockwise, from east, or from the destination rather than clockwise from north at the stated point
Gives a bearing without the required three-figure notation or omits a leading zero
Forms a scale factor using non-corresponding sides of similar shapes
Uses the enlargement scale factor in the reverse direction for the requested shape
Uses the linear scale factor directly for an area or volume instead of squaring or cubing it
Uses a constant difference between corresponding lengths instead of a constant multiplicative scale factor
Counts edges or diagonals as lines of symmetry without checking that reflection maps the shape onto itself
Gives the angle of rotation as the order, or omits the return at 360 degrees when counting the order
Infers a solid's planes or axes of symmetry from one two-dimensional view only
Uses 360 degrees on a straight line or 180 degrees around a point
Treats adjacent angles as vertically opposite, or assumes vertically opposite angles sum to 180 degrees
Uses the triangle angle sum for a quadrilateral or the quadrilateral angle sum for a triangle
Confuses corresponding, alternate and co-interior angle relationships
Sets co-interior angles equal instead of making them sum to 180 degrees
Uses n times 180 degrees instead of (n - 2) times 180 degrees for the interior-angle sum
Divides an angle sum equally among vertices of a polygon that is not stated to be regular
Fails to use the right angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact
Halves the angle at the circumference or doubles the angle at the centre instead of using centre equals twice circumference
Uses equal same-segment angles where opposite cyclic-quadrilateral angles should sum to 180 degrees, or the reverse
Matches the tangent angle to an angle subtended by the wrong chord in the alternate segment
Assumes chords are equal without establishing equal distance from the centre, or compares distance to chord endpoints rather than perpendicular distance
Uses a non-perpendicular chord bisector or fails to pass the perpendicular bisector through the circle's centre
Treats the two tangent lengths from the same external point as unrelated or includes radii as part of those lengths
Multiplies when converting to a larger metric unit or divides when converting to a smaller one
Uses a linear conversion factor for square or cubic units instead of squaring or cubing it
Uses an incorrect relationship between litres, millilitres and cubic centimetres
Calculates boundary length when area is required, or area when perimeter is required
Uses base times height for a triangle without the factor one half
Uses a sloping side instead of the perpendicular height in an area formula
Uses the circumference formula for area or the area formula for circumference
Uses pi times the radius rather than pi times the square of the radius for circle area
Uses 360 divided by the sector angle instead of sector angle divided by 360
Uses circle area for arc length or circumference for sector area
Omits an exposed face or counts a face more than once when finding surface area
Uses base area times height for a pyramid or cone without the factor one third
Uses a side face or a length instead of the constant cross-sectional area in prism volume
Adds component measures without removing an overlap or internal part that has been counted twice
Subtracts the larger component from the smaller one or removes the wrong missing region
Includes joined internal faces when calculating the external surface area of a compound solid
Reports an area in linear or cubic units, or a volume in linear or square units
Treats a shorter side as the hypotenuse instead of identifying the side opposite the right angle
Adds the squared sides when finding a shorter side, or subtracts when finding the hypotenuse
Applies Pythagoras' theorem to a triangle without a right angle
Chooses sine, cosine or tangent using sides labelled relative to the wrong reference angle
Uses a trigonometric ratio directly instead of its inverse when finding an angle
Uses a length that is not part of the selected right triangle or fails to find a required intermediate component
Chooses a sloping or along-line distance instead of the perpendicular distance from the point to the line
Measures an angle of elevation or depression from the vertical instead of the horizontal
Fails to transfer an angle of elevation or depression between parallel horizontal lines using alternate angles
Pairs a side with an angle that is not opposite it when applying the sine rule
Switches between side-over-sine and sine-over-side within the same sine-rule equation
Uses the wrong sign for the cosine term or substitutes the angle opposite the wrong side
Uses ab sin C without the factor one half
Uses an angle that is not included between the two chosen sides in the sine area formula
Uses a face diagonal as the required space diagonal, or combines lengths that do not form one right triangle
Finds the angle with a convenient edge rather than the angle between the line and its perpendicular projection on the plane
Moves every point by a fixed vector instead of placing image points the same perpendicular distance across the mirror line
Places an image point at a different perpendicular distance from the mirror line than its object point
Rotates clockwise when anticlockwise is required, or the reverse
Rotates around the origin or the shape's centre instead of the stated centre of rotation
Multiplies coordinates from the origin instead of enlarging along rays from the stated centre
Adds the scale factor to lengths or coordinates instead of multiplying distances from the centre
Moves in the opposite horizontal or vertical direction from the signs in the translation vector
Uses the top vector component vertically and the bottom component horizontally
Reverses the start and end points of a directed segment and therefore changes the vector's sign
Combines a horizontal component with a vertical component instead of adding corresponding components
Subtracts vectors in the reverse order and obtains the opposite vector
Multiplies only one component of a vector by the scalar
Adds the vector components or their absolute values instead of using the square root of the sum of their squares
Stops at the sum of squared components without taking its square root
Treats opposite directed line segments as the same vector because their lengths are equal
Uses a point's position vector as the displacement between two non-origin points without subtracting
Traverses a vector route against an arrow without changing that vector's sign
Estimates vector coefficients from the appearance of a diagram instead of using the stated ratios or algebra
Claims vectors are parallel without showing that one is a scalar multiple of the other
Gives a probability below zero or above one without recognising that it is impossible
Associates probability one with an impossible event or probability zero with a certain event
Uses event notation as an outcome value, or writes an event itself where its probability is required
Uses the number of favourable outcomes as the denominator or ignores some equally likely outcomes in the total
Counts outcomes as equally likely when the experiment or representation gives them different probabilities
Uses the same probability, subtracts from 100 without percentage units, or adds to one when finding a complement
Treats an experimental relative frequency as an exact theoretical probability that cannot vary between trials
Divides the event frequency by a category frequency rather than by the total number of trials
Divides the number of trials by the probability instead of multiplying them
Reports the probability itself as the expected frequency without applying the number of trials
Adds probabilities for successive 'and' events or multiplies mutually exclusive 'or' alternatives
Assigns probabilities from the same tree node that do not sum to one
Keeps the same denominator or event counts after an item is selected without replacement
Includes only one valid path or double-counts overlapping outcomes when combining events
Uses the original sample space after given information has restricted the possible outcomes
Classifies measured continuous data as discrete, or counted discrete data as continuous
Classifies categories as numerical measurements or numerical values as qualitative labels
Copies tally marks or raw values without converting them into correct class frequencies
Reads from the wrong row, column, key or category in a statistical table or diagram
Compares data sets using only an average and ignores the spread or consistency required for a valid comparison
Interprets a larger range or interquartile range as greater consistency rather than greater spread
Concludes that one variable causes the other solely because the data show correlation
Generalises from a small, biased or unrepresentative sample without acknowledging the limitation
Calculates or identifies the wrong average for mean, median or mode
Divides a total by the number of distinct values or classes instead of by the total frequency
Uses n divided by 2 without handling ordered positions correctly, especially for an even number of values
Subtracts the smallest frequency from the largest frequency instead of using the data values
Uses a class endpoint or width instead of the class midpoint when estimating a grouped mean
Averages class midpoints without weighting them by their frequencies
Reports the midpoint or a single value instead of the interval with the greatest frequency or frequency density
Uses a frequency or percentage directly as a sector angle instead of scaling it to 360 degrees
Uses touching bars for categorical data or separated bars for continuous grouped data without justification
Counts symbols as single observations without applying the pictogram key or partial-symbol value
Joins scatter points in observation order as though they form a time series or function
Calls a downward trend positive correlation or an upward trend negative correlation
Judges correlation strength from the steepness of a trend rather than how closely points cluster around it
Draws a point-to-point path or forces the line through particular points instead of balancing the scatter
Forces the line of best fit through the origin when the scatter does not support it
Treats a prediction far outside the observed data range as equally reliable as interpolation
Plots or lists ordinary class frequencies instead of running cumulative totals
Plots cumulative frequency at class midpoints or lower boundaries instead of the relevant upper class boundaries
Uses fixed positions such as 25, 50 and 75 rather than fractions of the actual total frequency
Adds the quartiles or subtracts them in reverse instead of calculating upper quartile minus lower quartile
Uses frequency as bar height when unequal class widths require frequency density
Counts grid squares or bar appearance instead of calculating class width from the class boundaries
Divides class width by frequency instead of frequency by class width
Treats bar height alone as proportional to frequency and ignores that histogram bar area represents frequency
